messages.body_plain:
That's helpful.  So here's what is going on.

The NIMBLE compiler, what we call the C++ code-generation system, does its best to look at types of objects created in setup code and used in run code or other methods.  It needed to decide what static C++ type to create for each R object.

In the case of matrix, the default element type of R's matrix() is logical:

storage.mode(matrix(nrow = 2, ncol = 2)) ## "logical"

What is really needed is to create a matrix in R with double (or integer, if you want) elements in your setup code.  When you assign some elements to c(0.9, 0.9), that happens dynamically in R, so by the time NIMBLE inspects it, it has storage.mode "double".

Another option would be

matrix(numeric(), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)

which we can see has double-precision elements.

storage.mode(matrix(numeric(), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)) # "double"

When your run code has a vectorized operation, nimble generates C++ that uses the Eigen library, and to do so it attempts to generate C++ that converts between types explicitly, which is needed in writing Eigen code.  That is when the error messages about loss of type information are generated.  I want to take a closer look because the way it errored out on you was not very friendly.

When your run code has only scalar assignments, nimble generates C++ that relies on automatic type-casting in C/C++. That is, scalar assignment from a logical to a double, for example, will compile but will not give you what you want, which is what you observed.

So the practical point of the story is to ensure that objects created in setup code that you need to use as double-precision are in fact double precision in R.

You can create a matrix in run code with nimMatrix (which "matrix" will automatically be converted to), which provides some more fine-grained control, so be sure to read help(nimMatrix).  But if you create it in setup code, it will persist across run calls, like member data of an object.

HTH.
-Perry

messages.subject: Issues using MS m-array model from jags in nimble
messages.subject_clean: Issues using MS m-array model from jags in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am new to Nimble - I took a workshop back at TWS in Reno but that has been my only introduction to the program. I am hoping to use Nimble to fit an integrated population model I have been working on for some time in Jags. By all accounts, the model should converge (I have checked with simulated data, sub-models, used informative priors/inits, etc.) but after 500k iterations, two parameters (which happen to have the most data) just will not converge. So, I am hoping to get this model up and running in Nimble to customize some samplers and see if it will work there.

I am using a multi-state m-array to fit my survival sub-model and am having an issue transitioning from the jags code to fitting the model in Nimble. I have attached the code I am working with (ipm_nimble.R). I am getting the following error:

Error in replaceConstantsRecurse(x, constEnv, constNames) :
  Error, hit end
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In replaceConstantsRecurse(x, constEnv, constNames) :
  Code ones was given as known but evaluates to a non-scalar.  This is probably not what you want.
2: In replaceConstantsRecurse(x, constEnv, constNames) :
  Code ones was given as known but evaluates to a non-scalar.  This is probably not what you want.
3: In replaceConstantsRecurse(x, constEnv, constNames) :
  Code zero was given as known but evaluates to a non-scalar.  This is probably not what you want.

I expect these errors refer specifically to Defining the cell probabilities of the m-array (specifically lines 239, 244, 259). Code was adapted from Kery and Schaub. I apologize if this is an elementary level question. Any help you could provide would be immensely helpful!

Kylee Dunham

Hi Kylee,

I suggest two resources for you, both linked from our documentation page: https://r-nimble.org/documentation-2

The first is the blog post on converting from JAGS to NIMBLE.  For your declarations involving "zero" and "ones" on the right-hand side, you will need explicit indexing, such as "zero[1:ns, 1:ns]".  There may be other issues, but those jump out as relevant from the error messages and looking at your code.

The second is the nimbleEcology package, which includes Hidden Markov Model distributions relevant for multi-state mark-recapture: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nimbleEcology/index.html

I think most people end up switching away from writing code out to a file and instead using nimbleCode within R.

HTH
-Perry

Instead of
 U[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns), (j-1)*ns+(1:ns)]
please try
 U[ ((t-1)*ns+1):((t-1)*ns + ns), ((j-1)*ns+1):((j-1)*ns + ns)]
(which I guess is the same as:
 U[ ((t-1)*ns+1):(t*ns), ((j-1)*ns+1):(j*ns)]
)
and similar in other places.

-Perry

messages.subject: Subset of nodes not updating when using dmulti
messages.subject_clean: Subset of nodes not updating when using dmulti
messages.body_plain:
Dear NIMBLE-Team,

I have recently been working on the implementation of a somewhat more complex integrated population model using NIMBLE.
Unlike other such models I worked with previously, this one includes not just two potential transitions for individuals in the population (i.e. survive or die), but multiple (i.e. transition to >2 states possible).
As such, I am implementing the process model using multinomial likelihoods. However, I have run into a problem where some (but not all!) of the stochastic nodes described by the multinomial likelihood are not updated at all (they simply remain "stuck" at the initial values).

No matter what I tried, I could not get these nodes to update and have a feeling I must be missing something important here. It would be fantastic if you could take a look into the problem and help me out!

I have made a reproducible example of the problem, and upload it here.
Below, I'll write down some more information on the specific problem.

Any tips/suggestions would be much appreciated!

Cheers,

Chloé

********************************************************************************************************
ADDITIONAL INFO ON PROBLEM:

In the process model, population size and structure are represented as N[zo, zt, t], where zt is the current state ("target state"), zo is the previous state ("origin state").
For the example (and the IPM application I am working on), states 1-3 are alive individuals, while states 4-9 are different "types" of dead individuals.
This means that only individuals in states 1, 2, and 3 at time t can contribute to population size at time t+1.
In the model, I specify this as:

    for(z in 1:3){
        N[z, 1:9, t+1] ~ dmulti(p = U[z, 1:9, t], size = sum(N[1:3, z, t]))
    }

When t <= Tmax, all nodes N[z, 4:9, t] are being updated, but all nodes N[z, 1:3, t] are not and remain "stuck" at the same values.
This happens irrespective of whether initial values are provided for N, and independent of assumptions about prior distribution of initial numbers (N[z, 1:9, 1])
Funnily enough, at the last time-step, all nodes N[z, 1:9, Tmax+1] are updated.

In the example, I provide the transition probabilities U as data. In the practical implementation (the integrated population model), U and (parts of) N are estimated from data.
However, the problem of "stuck" nodes is exactly the same there, so I assume if it can be "fixed" in the small example I provide, it can also be fixed in the integrated model.

Side note:
I ran the example using R 4.0.0 and nimble_0.9.0

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Firstly, I'm really excited about NIMBLE. It's been a while since I've played around with BUGS and I'm really diggin' the work you folks have done on NIMBLE. Great stuff.

I have what is a relatively simple model that includes an indicator for model selection. I followed the reversible jump example and everything seems to be working but when I try to extract the samples of the indicator they are completely gone.

Here's what I mean:

R> unique(sub('\\[[0-9]+\\]', '', colnames(samples_rj)))
[1] "dispersion" "psi"        "shift"      "t_lower"    "t_upper"

'shift' has an indicator going into it (z) which is not appearing in the samples. psi is the prior on z which actually does appear in the samples.

here's how I configured the RJ sampler:

configureRJ(conf = full_configuration,
  targetNodes = c('shift'),
  indicatorNodes = c('z'),
  control = list(mean = 0, scale = 1)
  )

And here is the actual model:

full_code = nimbleCode({
  dispersion ~ dexp(1 / 200)
  for (n in 1:N) {
    t_lower[n] ~ dnorm(-1.04, sd = 1)
    t_upper[n] ~ dnorm(1.04, sd = 1)
    constraint[n] ~ dconstraint(t_lower[n] < t_upper[n])
  }

  psi ~ dbeta(1, 1)
  for (g in 1:G) {
    z[g] ~ dbern(psi)
    # z[g] <- zi[g] * (1 - nt_control[g])
    shift[g] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    for (n in 1:N) {
      q[n, g, 1] <- phi(t_lower[n] - z[g] * shift[g])
      q[n, g, 3] <- 1 - phi(t_upper[n] - z[g] * shift[g])
      q[n, g, 2] <- 1 - q[n, g, 3] - q[n, g, 1]
      alpha[n, g, 1:3] <- dispersion * q[n, g, 1:3]

      x[n, g, 1:3] ~ ddirchmulti(alpha[n, g, 1:3], x_total[n, g])
    }
  }
})

Would appreciate any feedback you might have.

Thanks in advance!

Best,

Harold

messages.body_plain:
Hi Harold,

Happy to hear you are trying out NIMBLE and the reversible jump!

About your problem, is the indicator variable z in the monitors?

Only variables that are monitored will have their samples saved for use outside of the MCMC. From your example, you can check which variables are monitored via   full_configuration$monitors() and in case add the indicator variables via full_configuration$addMonitors('z').

The default MCMC configuration includes monitors on all top-level stochastic nodes of the model, and I think that the indicator variables would not be included by default.

Let me know if this works!

Best,

Sally

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chloé

As far as I can see, the problem appears to arise from the auto-correlation generated by the markovian dynamics of your model. Adding time to your code chunk (as you do in your file) we have this...

for(t in 1:Tmax){

    for(z in 1:3){
        N[z, 1:9, t+1] ~ dmulti(p = U[z, 1:9, t], size = sum(N[1:3, z, t]))
    }

}

The sampler for multinomial nodes performs Metropolis-Hastings updates, i.e. it will propose an alternative vector for N[z, 1:9, t+1], evaluate the likelihood, and accept/reject based on the Metropolis-Hastings ratio.

With your model, when a sampler generates a proposal for N[z, 1:9, t], it will be very likely that it will generate a new value for the "size" argument in the following time step, i.e. sum(N[1:3, z, t+1]). But if that value changes then the multinomial likelihood of the following timestep is no longer valid. So the proposal will be rejected.

To illustrate this consider the following R code

> (r <- rmultinom(1, size=10, prob=1:4))
     [,1]
[1,]    2
[2,]    1
[3,]    3
[4,]    4
> dmultinom(r, size=10, prob=1:4)
[1] 0.01741824
> dmultinom(r, size=11, prob=1:4)
Error in dmultinom(r, size = 11, prob = 1:4) :
  size != sum(x), i.e. one is wrong
> dmultinom(r, size=9, prob=1:4)
Error in dmultinom(r, size = 9, prob = 1:4) :
  size != sum(x), i.e. one is wrong

So the default sampler for your multinomial nodes does not stand a chance. You will need an alternative way to generate proposals that can account for the autocorrelation in your model.

David

hi Vincent,

Parallelization with NIMBLE is a bit tricky (we have plans to improve this in the long-term) because of how our C++ objects are managed from within R. We have an example on our webpage that discusses this and shows how to do things. Can you take a look at that and let us know if modifying what you are doing based on that doesn't work?

https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html

In particular, you can't use a fork cluster. If you have been using a fork cluster it would be surprising if it ever worked.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi David!

Thank you very much for your reply, this makes a lot of sense.
It also explains why I only got this issue when using the multinomial likelihood with a "size" that is estimated (when "size" is a fixed constant, i.e. given as data, there was no problem).

I am now wondering what would be the best way to go about circumventing this problem.
>From my view, this can be approached either by changing the samplers, or changing the model structure.

Samplers:
I assume none of the other "pre-programmed" samplers in the r-nimble package would be able to deal with this? Could there be a solution involving block sampling?
Surely, some samplers for autoregressive multinomial likelihoods must have been developed? Is anyone aware of examples?
I would greatly appreciate any pointers towards already existing solutions, or for building a custom sampler to deal with this.

Model structure:
Alternatively, getting rid of the autoregressive multinomial likelihood may solve the problem.
The obvious way of doing this seems to be rewriting the model as sequential (and conditional) binomial likelihoods. However, this is not just inelegant, but kind of defeats the purpose of what we would like to do with this model in practice ("general" integrated population model allowing for >2 transitions conditional on survival).
Are there any alternative formulations for the model that I may not be thinking of at the moment?

Any thoughts, ideas, and references (from anyone!) very welcome!

Cheers,

Chloé

messages.body_plain: I'm fitting a ton of models using Nimble on a Microsoft Azure VM in a Docker container. I'm iterating through around 2200 models, but I'm finding that as more and more models are fit, my disk space is being eaten up (to the point that it ends up 100% full). Once I kill the docker container, disk space frees back up, and I can pick up where I left off. Presumably there are files (that are adding up to over 20GB) being written somewhere within the container. I am writing some outputs, but only about 2GB worth, and it's to a separate volume-mounted drive. Any idea what might be going on? I'm running the models in parallel with foreach %dopar%. Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Does Nimble write any sort of temporary files to disk?
messages.subject_clean: Does Nimble write any sort of temporary files to disk?
messages.body_plain:
Yes.  compileNimble writes C++ code, compiles it, and links it to a  static library that comes with nimble, each result in files.  Also there is a once-per-session compilation step, which is why the first call to compileNimble is always slower than subsequent calls.  The files are normally placed in tempdir(), the temporary directory automatically created by R for each session that is available for use by packages (or the user) and cleaned up upon R exit (usually).  One option would be for you to iterate through your models such that you invoke a new R session for each model.  For example, you could have a primary R session (or other script) that uses system2 to call Rscript to run one case.  That would create separate R process for each case, which should clean up its own tempdir() upon exit.   Another option would be to control where nimble puts its files by using the dirName argument to compileNimble and then adding a step in your code that removes files (curiously named unlink() in R) from wherever you put them.  They shouldn't need to be retained after compileNimble has finished.  If you use that option, you might also want to use nimble:::clearCompiled(obj) after each case, where obj is any object associated with one nimble project, such as the model.  That will attempt to clear memory of the C++ objects from that nimble project.
HTH
-Perry

It's great to see this, Simona.

We try to capture output and show it, but sometimes that doesn't work as we expect.  To see more of the C++ output, try going to the tempdir() (or use dirName argument to control where files are put) and looking for the .log and .err files with a name that you see in the C++ compiler call shown.  If it's hard to follow, you can watch the set of files get created once you have tempdir() open.  Feel free to share that.  I'm pressed for time today but would be happy to help iron this out with you.

-Perry

> >
> > On Thursday, June 18, 2020 at 2:09:31 PM UTC-6, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > Yes.  compileNimble writes C++ code, compiles it, and links it to a  static library that comes with nimble, each result in files.  Also there is a once-per-session compilation step, which is why the first call to compileNimble is always slower than subsequent calls.  The files are normally placed in tempdir(), the temporary directory automatically created by R for each session that is available for use by packages (or the user) and cleaned up upon R exit (usually).  One option would be for you to iterate through your models such that you invoke a new R session for each model.  For example, you could have a primary R session (or other script) that uses system2 to call Rscript to run one case.  That would create separate R process for each case, which should clean up its own tempdir() upon exit.   Another option would be to control where nimble puts its files by using the dirName argument to compileNimble and then adding a step in your code that removes files (curiously named unlink() in R) from wherever you put them.  They shouldn't need to be retained after compileNimble has finished.  If you use that option, you might also want to use nimble:::clearCompiled(obj) after each case, where obj is any object associated with one nimble project, such as the model.  That will attempt to clear memory of the C++ objects from that nimble project.

messages.subject: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
messages.subject_clean: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is a follow up to my post https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/nimble-users/b8G-1MtTm-c/smrwlsTUBAAJ which was about how to sum a parameter vector across neighbors.

The solution we came up with was to use a Nimble function,

nei_sum <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(param = double(1), adj = double(1), count = double(1), num = double(1), i = double(0)) {

    return(sum(param[adj[count[i]:(count[i]+num[i]-1)]]))

    returnType(double(0))

  })

Here, param is the parameter vector, adj is a vector of neighbors, count is the starting index and num is the number of neighbors. This works computationally but creates many unnecessary dependencies in the model and probably greatly increases run time.

Take this as a simple example. Say we have a parameter vector S[1:N] and we create the nodes

for(i in 1:N){
   neisum[i] <-  nei_sum(param=S[1:N],adj=adj[1:L],count=count[1:N],num=num[1:N],i=i)
}

neisum[i] is the sum of S[1:N] across the neighbors of i. Consider i=1 and suppose that locations 2 and 5 are neighbors of location 1. Then neisum[1] is equivalent to

neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]

The problem is that with the correct dependency structure only S[2] and S[5] should have neisum[1] as a dependency. However, with the nei_sum function all the S have neisum[1] as a dependency. So, for example, if you update S[6] it will update neisum[1] even though in reality there is no connection. Obviously, in very large models this could greatly increase the run time and have ripple effects if there are further dependencies of the neisum[i]s.

So far I can only think of two solutions which are not really satisfactory. First you could just write out each sum manually like so,

neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
neisum[2] <- ....
.
.
.
neisum[N] <- ...

I think this should work well it is just a bit janky to write it line by line. In my case I have 160 locations so its 160 lines added to the model. Imagine if you have 1000s of locations?

A second solution would be to rewrite all the samplers that update S and fix the dependencies in the setup. I do not really like this solution either but it would scale better with the number of locations.

Can anyone think of a better solution?

messages.subject: storing sums of log probabilities
messages.subject_clean: storing sums of log probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

We've had a question on twitter about recording the sums of log probabilities (https://twitter.com/fbuderman/status/1272951989228445698).  This has come up before and might be something in need of a more general solution.  Any input on use cases?

Meanwhile, here is a workaround that uses a proxy sampler (i.e. not really an MCMC sampler, but invoked via the list of samplers) to record the sum of arbitrary log probabilities.  The default is to include all stochastic nodes, but any nodes can be specified.  Multiple of these can be included.

-Perry

-----

library(nimble)

# A proxy "sampler" that isn't really an MCMC sampler but will be called
# in the list of samplers.  It will store the sum of nodes give in control$logProbNodes
# in the target node.
storeLogProb <- nimbleFunction(
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    logProbNodes <- model$expandNodeNames(control[['logProbNodes']])
  },
  run = function() {
    sumLogProb <- model$getLogProb(logProbNodes)
    model[[target]] <<- sumLogProb
  },
  methods = list(reset = function() {})
)

# A utility function to modify an mcmc configuration to use storeLogProb.
# Arguments are:
# mcmcConf: an mcmc configuration such as returned by configureMCMC
# model:    an uncompiled model object
# target:   the node name to be used for storing the sum of log probabilities
# nodes:    the nodes whose sum of log probabilities will be stored in the target node.
#           default value for nodes is all stochastic nodes in the model (except target).
configureStoreLogProb <- function(mcmcConf, model, target, nodes) {
  if(missing(nodes))
    nodes <- model$getNodeNames(stochOnly = TRUE)
  nodes <- nodes[ nodes != target ]
  mcmcConf$removeSamplers(target)
  mcmcConf$addSampler(type = 'storeLogProb', target = target, control = list(logProbNodes = nodes))
  mcmcConf
}

# Example:
# This model will have real nodes a[1]...a[10] (a toy with no data, but that doesn't matter for demonstration  of storeLogProb).
# And it will have a proxy node "sumLogProb" that will be used for recording the sum of log probabilities
modelCode <- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:10) a[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  sumLogProb ~ dnorm(0,1) ## dnorm(0,1) will not be used.  It just establishes sumLogProb as a stochastic node.
})

model <- nimbleModel(modelCode, inits = list(a = rnorm(10), sumLogProb = 0))
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(model)
configureStoreLogProb(mcmcConf, model, 'sumLogProb')
mcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)

cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
cmcmc <- compileNimble(mcmc, project = model)
samples <- runMCMC(cmcmc, niter = 10)
samples[,'sumLogProb']

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chloe,

I've given this a little more thought.  I think I see the purpose of how you have set things up.  Unfortunately, it does not seem like an easy problem to solve. The current dmulti sampler conditions on size.  I think an update at one step could make the next step impossible by creating a mismatch between the size of the dmulti and the resulting states.  For example, if N[z, 1:9, t] is updated in a way that moves some individuals from alive states to dead states, then sum(N[1:3, z, t]) will no longer match the sum of the random variable it defines, namely sum(N[z, 1:9, t+1]).  I don't know if you've made any progress reformulating the model based on the twitter thread.  I imagine it would be possible to sample this model with a custom sampler that respects the constraints involved.   I don't think a vanilla block sampler will work.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,

Setting aside issues of cyclic graphs (which won't work), here are a couple of other inelegant but perhaps slightly more appealing solutions to sum over neighbor sets without creating unnecessary dependencies.

Option 1:
If you can break the neighbor indices into sets grouped by number of neighbors, and if there aren't ever a huge number of neighbors, you could do something like this
# neighbor_indices[i, j] is the jth neighbor of cell i
# two neighbors:
for(i in 1:number_of_cells_with_two_neighbors)  {
  neisum[ two_neighbor_cells[i] ] <- S[ neighbor_indices[ three_neighbor_cells[i], 1] ] + S[ neighbor_indices[three_neighbor_cells[i], 2] ]
}

# three neighbors:
for(i in 1:number_of_cells_with_three_neighbors)  {
  neisum[ three_neighbor_cells[i] ] <- S[ neighbor_indices[ three_neighbor_cells[i], 1] ] + S[ neighbor_indices[three_neighbor_cells[i], 2] ] + S[ neighbor_indices[three_neighbor_cells[i], 3] ]
}
# etc.

# Option 2:
for(i in 1:num_cells) {
  reisum[i, num_neighbors[i] ] <- S[ neighbor_indices[i, num_neighbors[i] ] ]
  for(j in 2:num_neighbors[i]) {
     neisum[i, j-1] <- neisum[i, j] + S[ neighbor_indices[i, j-1] ]
  }
}
# Result is that neisum[i, j] is the sum from j to the last neighbor of cell 1, so neisum[i, 1] is the sum of all neighbors of cell i

Option 1 uses more code but creates fewer dependencies in the model graph.
Option 2 uses less code but creates sequences of deterministic dependencies that, if they are very long, can bog down some steps, particularly conjugacy checking.  If you don't need conjugacy checking, you can set useConjugacy=FALSE in configureMCMC.

I haven't tested these.  It's highly possible I glitched the indexing, but I hope the ideas are clear.

This is an interesting problem for the design of the system - something to think about.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Just a couple of quick thoughts.

I imagine it should be possible to set up a sampler for sampling a series of dependant multinomial nodes. I suggest this is written as a separate chunk of code so that the current sampler remains unchanged. In which case there would (ideally) need to be some complimentary work on how nimble chooses between the current sampler and a sequential-multinomial sampler (that said, a user can always modify which samplers are being use manually).

Chloé, will the number of time steps remain the same or be much bigger in your final model? This is an important detail, because, whilst the tailored (sequential-multinomial) sampler idea might work OK for a modest number of time steps, it's performance can be expected to decline as the number of time steps increases. In which case an approach based on particle MCMC (PMCMC) is probably more appropriate. I've not checked to see if nimble's current PMCMC functionality is capable of handling multinomial nodes.

Best
David

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry

Many thanks for this - it's a great solution!!

For models where convergence to the target distribution is slow, tracking sumLogProbs provides a simple indication of whether you should extend the burn-in period. In these cases, I'll often write a loop that will perform a chunk of burn-in and then check if there is a non-negligible trend in sumLogProbs to decide if further burn-in chunks are required.

I'm currently collaborating with a team that have mixing issues with a model that has a very large number of latent variables. My current approach of tracking logProbs for all the latent variables (and using rowSums after doing MCMC) uses a huge amount of RAM. Your solution will greatly reduce the memory requirements in this work.

Best
David

messages.body_plain:
Hi again Perry!

Thank you very much for looking into this. All of us (David from above, me, and you) seem to agree about where the problem is most likely coming from, and it does look like solving it will require to write a custom sampler that works on autocorrelated multinomial nodes, i.e. does not condition on the size argument.
I think having such a sampler would be useful not just for me and this specific problem, but also for other users (working with more complex population models, and possibly other kinds of models as well), and I would very much like to give it a try.

While my knowledge of MCMC samplers is rather limited at the moment, I am keen on learning more.
Would you - or other members of the NIMBLE team - be interested in helping me with this, at least in the beginning? Would be happy to chat, as it's also ISEC at the moment!
(Any pointers towards relevant literature and/or examples to get started would be much appreciated too!)

Cheers,

Chloé

> Hi Chloe,
>
> I've given this a little more thought.  I think I see the purpose of how you have set things up.  Unfortunately, it does not seem like an easy problem to solve. The current dmulti sampler conditions on size.  I think an update at one step could make the next step impossible by creating a mismatch between the size of the dmulti and the resulting states.  For example, if N[z, 1:9, t] is updated in a way that moves some individuals from alive states to dead states, then sum(N[1:3, z, t]) will no longer match the sum of the random variable it defines, namely sum(N[z, 1:9, t+1]).  I don't know if you've made any progress reformulating the model based on the twitter thread.  I imagine it would be possible to sample this model with a custom sampler that respects the constraints involved.   I don't think a vanilla block sampler will work.
>
> -Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,
This is great! Thank you for addressing my question and providing a workaround solution.
-Franny

On Sunday, June 21, 2020 at 7:57:02 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
> We've had a question on twitter about recording the sums of log probabilities (https://twitter.com/fbuderman/status/1272951989228445698).  This has come up before and might be something in need of a more general solution.  Any input on use cases?
>
> Meanwhile, here is a workaround that uses a proxy sampler (i.e. not really an MCMC sampler, but invoked via the list of samplers) to record the sum of arbitrary log probabilities.  The default is to include all stochastic nodes, but any nodes can be specified.  Multiple of these can be included.
>
> -Perry
>
> -----
>
> library(nimble)
>
> # A proxy "sampler" that isn't really an MCMC sampler but will be called
> # in the list of samplers.  It will store the sum of nodes give in control$logProbNodes
> # in the target node.
> storeLogProb <- nimbleFunction(
>   contains = sampler_BASE,
>   setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
>     logProbNodes <- model$expandNodeNames(control[['logProbNodes']])
>   },
>   run = function() {
>     sumLogProb <- model$getLogProb(logProbNodes)
>     model[[target]] <<- sumLogProb
>   },
>   methods = list(reset = function() {})
> )
>
> # A utility function to modify an mcmc configuration to use storeLogProb.
> # Arguments are:
> # mcmcConf: an mcmc configuration such as returned by configureMCMC
> # model:    an uncompiled model object
> # target:   the node name to be used for storing the sum of log probabilities
> # nodes:    the nodes whose sum of log probabilities will be stored in the target node.
> #           default value for nodes is all stochastic nodes in the model (except target).
> configureStoreLogProb <- function(mcmcConf, model, target, nodes) {
>   if(missing(nodes))
>     nodes <- model$getNodeNames(stochOnly = TRUE)
>   nodes <- nodes[ nodes != target ]
>   mcmcConf$removeSamplers(target)
>   mcmcConf$addSampler(type = 'storeLogProb', target = target, control = list(logProbNodes = nodes))
>   mcmcConf
> }
>
> # Example:
> # This model will have real nodes a[1]...a[10] (a toy with no data, but that doesn't matter for demonstration  of storeLogProb).
> # And it will have a proxy node "sumLogProb" that will be used for recording the sum of log probabilities
> modelCode <- nimbleCode({
>   for(i in 1:10) a[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
>   sumLogProb ~ dnorm(0,1) ## dnorm(0,1) will not be used.  It just establishes sumLogProb as a stochastic node.
> })
>
> model <- nimbleModel(modelCode, inits = list(a = rnorm(10), sumLogProb = 0))
> mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> configureStoreLogProb(mcmcConf, model, 'sumLogProb')
> mcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
>
> cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> cmcmc <- compileNimble(mcmc, project = model)
> samples <- runMCMC(cmcmc, niter = 10)
> samples[,'sumLogProb']

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Perry!

Your second solution worked really well. I used a slightly different coding

      Snei[num[i],i] <- S[adj[count[i]]]
      for(j in 2:num[i]){
        Snei[num[i]-j+1,i] <- Snei[num[i]-j+2,i] + S[adj[count[i]+j-1]]
      }

Only thing I am confused about is how the backward indexing works? In some cases num[i]=1 so the for loop would be for(j in 2:1). I am guessing it just doesn't run the loop in these cases since it seemed to return the correct sum.

This reduced the run time of my model from 6.5 hours to 1 hour so it is a massive improvement!

About the cyclical graph, I think that could be a really great use case for this. My understanding is that some models are best specified with a cyclical graph, like the Leroux model, although it does not always lead to a valid model. It would be interesting if you could specify a cyclical graph and Nimble would be able to decide if it was valid and form some samplers, maybe even using pseudo likelihood if necessary. Then you could fit general markov random field models in Nimble. See this paper for a good example of the type of models I am talking about, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/env.2427.

Although in my case I do not have a cyclical graph. I have another important use case of lagged dependence in a spatio-temporal model. I think Andrew Lawson talked about this in the previous thread and he has some papers on it.

On Saturday, June 20, 2020 at 12:44:35 PM UTC-4, Dirk Douwes-Schultz wrote:
> Hi,
>
> This is a follow up to my post https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/nimble-users/b8G-1MtTm-c/smrwlsTUBAAJ which was about how to sum a parameter vector across neighbors.
>
> The solution we came up with was to use a Nimble function,
>
> nei_sum <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(param = double(1), adj = double(1), count = double(1), num = double(1), i = double(0)) {
>
>     return(sum(param[adj[count[i]:(count[i]+num[i]-1)]]))
>
>     returnType(double(0))
>
>   })
>
> Here, param is the parameter vector, adj is a vector of neighbors, count is the starting index and num is the number of neighbors. This works computationally but creates many unnecessary dependencies in the model and probably greatly increases run time.
>
> Take this as a simple example. Say we have a parameter vector S[1:N] and we create the nodes
>
> for(i in 1:N){
>    neisum[i] <-  nei_sum(param=S[1:N],adj=adj[1:L],count=count[1:N],num=num[1:N],i=i)
> }
>
> neisum[i] is the sum of S[1:N] across the neighbors of i. Consider i=1 and suppose that locations 2 and 5 are neighbors of location 1. Then neisum[1] is equivalent to
>
> neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
>
> The problem is that with the correct dependency structure only S[2] and S[5] should have neisum[1] as a dependency. However, with the nei_sum function all the S have neisum[1] as a dependency. So, for example, if you update S[6] it will update neisum[1] even though in reality there is no connection. Obviously, in very large models this could greatly increase the run time and have ripple effects if there are further dependencies of the neisum[i]s.
>
> So far I can only think of two solutions which are not really satisfactory. First you could just write out each sum manually like so,
>
> neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
> neisum[2] <- ....
> .
> .
> .
> neisum[N] <- ...
>
> I think this should work well it is just a bit janky to write it line by line. In my case I have 160 locations so its 160 lines added to the model. Imagine if you have 1000s of locations?
>
> A second solution would be to rewrite all the samplers that update S and fix the dependencies in the setup. I do not really like this solution either but it would scale better with the number of locations.
>
> Can anyone think of a better solution?
>
>
>

That's a good point about the backward indexing.  I think a "2:1" case will not be included.  I think you could check with model$getDependencies("S[3]") if, for example, S[3] is the single neighbor in a case with num[i] = 1.

messages.body_plain:
Everyone don't forget the nimble system option: "processBackwardsModelIndexRanges"

The default value for this option is FALSE.  That means "backwards" indexing ranges in BUGS model definitions won't create any nodes (e.g., for(i in 5:1) x[i] ~ ....)

If you set:
nimbleOptions(processBackwardsModelIndexRanges = TRUE)

prior to model building, then the example above would in fact create 5 nodes: x[1], x[2], ... x[5].

On Tue, Jun 23, 2020 at 4:35 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

> Glad it worked!
>
> That's a good point about the backward indexing.  I think a "2:1" case will not be included.  I think you could check with model$getDependencies("S[3]") if, for example, S[3] is the single neighbor in a case with num[i] = 1.
>
> Thanks for the paper link.  The one thoroughly developed case of a cyclic graph in nimble is support for CAR models.  It's not clear to me how well one could automate handling of cyclic graphs, but I wonder if there is an intermediate (in generality) way to support them with some boost of information from the analyst.
>
> -Perry
>
>
> On Tue, Jun 23, 2020 at 12:59 PM Dirk Douwes-Schultz <dirkdouw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks Perry!
> >
> > Your second solution worked really well. I used a slightly different coding
> >
> >       Snei[num[i],i] <- S[adj[count[i]]]
> >       for(j in 2:num[i]){
> >         Snei[num[i]-j+1,i] <- Snei[num[i]-j+2,i] + S[adj[count[i]+j-1]]
> >       }
> >
> > Only thing I am confused about is how the backward indexing works? In some cases num[i]=1 so the for loop would be for(j in 2:1). I am guessing it just doesn't run the loop in these cases since it seemed to return the correct sum.
> >
> > This reduced the run time of my model from 6.5 hours to 1 hour so it is a massive improvement!
> >
> > About the cyclical graph, I think that could be a really great use case for this. My understanding is that some models are best specified with a cyclical graph, like the Leroux model, although it does not always lead to a valid model. It would be interesting if you could specify a cyclical graph and Nimble would be able to decide if it was valid and form some samplers, maybe even using pseudo likelihood if necessary. Then you could fit general markov random field models in Nimble. See this paper for a good example of the type of models I am talking about, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/env.2427.
> >
> > Although in my case I do not have a cyclical graph. I have another important use case of lagged dependence in a spatio-temporal model. I think Andrew Lawson talked about this in the previous thread and he has some papers on it.
> >
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, June 20, 2020 at 12:44:35 PM UTC-4, Dirk Douwes-Schultz wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > This is a follow up to my post https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/nimble-users/b8G-1MtTm-c/smrwlsTUBAAJ which was about how to sum a parameter vector across neighbors.
> > >
> > > The solution we came up with was to use a Nimble function,
> > >
> > > nei_sum <- nimbleFunction(
> > >   run = function(param = double(1), adj = double(1), count = double(1), num = double(1), i = double(0)) {
> > >
> > >     return(sum(param[adj[count[i]:(count[i]+num[i]-1)]]))
> > >
> > >     returnType(double(0))
> > >
> > >   })
> > >
> > > Here, param is the parameter vector, adj is a vector of neighbors, count is the starting index and num is the number of neighbors. This works computationally but creates many unnecessary dependencies in the model and probably greatly increases run time.
> > >
> > > Take this as a simple example. Say we have a parameter vector S[1:N] and we create the nodes
> > >
> > > for(i in 1:N){
> > >    neisum[i] <-  nei_sum(param=S[1:N],adj=adj[1:L],count=count[1:N],num=num[1:N],i=i)
> > > }
> > >
> > > neisum[i] is the sum of S[1:N] across the neighbors of i. Consider i=1 and suppose that locations 2 and 5 are neighbors of location 1. Then neisum[1] is equivalent to
> > >
> > > neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
> > >
> > > The problem is that with the correct dependency structure only S[2] and S[5] should have neisum[1] as a dependency. However, with the nei_sum function all the S have neisum[1] as a dependency. So, for example, if you update S[6] it will update neisum[1] even though in reality there is no connection. Obviously, in very large models this could greatly increase the run time and have ripple effects if there are further dependencies of the neisum[i]s.
> > >
> > > So far I can only think of two solutions which are not really satisfactory. First you could just write out each sum manually like so,
> > >
> > > neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
> > > neisum[2] <- ....
> > > .
> > > .
> > > .
> > > neisum[N] <- ...
> > >
> > > I think this should work well it is just a bit janky to write it line by line. In my case I have 160 locations so its 160 lines added to the model. Imagine if you have 1000s of locations?
> > >
> > > A second solution would be to rewrite all the samplers that update S and fix the dependencies in the setup. I do not really like this solution either but it would scale better with the number of locations.
> > >
> > > Can anyone think of a better solution?
> > >
> > >
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Daniel, so the model was working as intended.

Thanks for your comments Perry. I am not an expert on markov random fields, but I have read some papers on the topic. Here is one way you could form samplers for arbitrary cyclical graphs.

So, say you have a vector of nodes x=(x_1,...,x_N) that the user defines a cyclical graph over. This means the user specifies p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda) for i=1,...,N where lambda is some hyper parameters. Here x_(-i) are all x but x_i. Then the full conditional for x_i is p(x_i | x_(-i),  lambda, theta, y) which is proportional to p(y_i | x_i, theta)*p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda). Therefore, you can sample x_i one at a time using MH/binary/categorical etc. samplers, depending on the type of node.

Sampling lambda though is the bigger issue. p(lambda | x, theta, y) is proportional to p(x | lambda)*p(lambda) but p(x | lambda) might not even exist like with the CAR model. I think there are 3 cases to consider and this is where user input can come in. First in some proper Gaussian models you can go from  p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda) to p(x | lambda) using formulas. Secondly for improper models, I think you need to consider a sensible posterior kernel for lambda, maybe the user can supply this. Finally in some models, like potts model, p(x|lambda) exists but is too difficult to compute. In this case you can use pseudo likelihood, p(x|lambda) is substituted with the product of  p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda).

Again I am by no means an expert on this topic so if anyone has a better idea how to implement something like this please contribute.

messages.body_plain:
I’m learning Nimble and I am trying to replicate a model fit from R's glm, but my estimated parameters do not match (see parameter estimates further below).  I wonder if this is because I am handling factor variables (and their interactions) incorrectly in Nimble or if it is related to some parameters not mixing well in my Nimble model.

Questions: Is the discrepancy in estimated effects due to an incorrect model representation in Nimble or poor mixing in the MCMC chains?  More generally, how do I absorb one level of a factor into the intercept in Nimble?  Did I correctly code the interaction between age and gender?

Thanks for any guidance on this! Also please point me to any existing documentation that addresses these questions.

Brian

GLM:
fit~glm(wearing_mask~gender_factor + age_factor + gender_factor:age_factor,
            data=mydataWOna,family=binomial())

Nimble code:
maskCode4_0 <- nimbleCode({
  ### Priors
  intercept~dnorm(0,sd=1000)
  maleEffect~dnorm(0,sd = 1000)

  for(i in 1:4) {
    # Priors for age effect and age:male interaction
    if(i==1){
      ageEffect[i] <-0 # attempt to force 1st level of factor into intercept
      ageMaleI[i] <-0 # attempt to force 1st level of factor into intercept
    } else {
      ageEffect[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
      ageMaleI[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
    }
  }

  ### logit link and Bernoulli data probabilities
  for(i in 1:N) {
    logit(mask_prob[i]) <- intercept + maleEffect*male[i] +
      ageClassBase[i]*ageEffect[ageClass[i]] + male[i]*ageMaleI[ageClass[i]]
    mask[i] ~ dbern(mask_prob[i])
  }

})

Use of 'if' in model code is only for defining different models from one piece of code, not for defining logic of a single model.

You'd want to do something like this:

ageEffect[1] <- 0
ageMale[1] <- 0

      ageEffect[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
      ageMaleI[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)

What is happening right now is that presuming there is not an "i" that is set to 1 in your R global environment, the model is being defined with priors for i = 1,2,3,4 and not setting the values for the first element to be 0.

I didn't look any more closely at your code or results than just noticing that one issue. If after making the fix above, things still seem strange, feel free to write back.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a question about nimble's scalability for large n problems. Below is code for a very simple toy example of a simple logistic regression where n=1e+06. Ultimately, I'd like to obtain posterior samples from the posterior distribution p(b1,b2|z). Note that there are no large matrix operations (i.e., inverses, determinants) nor are we dealing with high-dimensional set of model parameters.

However, I am unable to even build an MCMC sampler due to the large size of the dataset. The process is shut down during the nimbleFunction() evaluation. For smaller datasets (n=3e+05), the bulk of the walltime is attributed to building the nimble model (highlighted below).  Once the model is built, everything else proceeds very smoothly.

Do you have any tips for using nimble with very large datasets? Is there a way to build the nimble models faster using nimbleFunction()?

Thank you so much.

Ben

#Toy Example

# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000
beta<-c(1,1)
XMat<-cbind(runif(n,-1,1),runif(n,-1,1))
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize
consts   <- list(n=n)
data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat)
inits    <- list(beta1=0,beta2=0)

# Model String
model_binary_string_conj <- nimbleCode({
  # Data Model
  for(i in 1:n){
    prob[i] <- exp(XB[i])/(1+exp(XB[i]))
    Z[i] ~ dbern(prob[i])
  }
  XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]

  # Parameter Model
  beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
  beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})

# Build Model
Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string_conj, data = data,
                    constants=consts, inits = inits)
cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)
RmodelConf$printSamplers()
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta1", "beta2"))
bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC)

# Run sampler
niter=1000
cMCMC$run(niter)
samples_extended <- as.matrix(cMCMC$mvSamples)

messages.body_plain:
Mike, when you configure the MCMC, usually a step using configureMCMC(), you could try adding the option:
configureMCMC(model, onlySlice = TRUE)

This will assign slice samplers for all non-conjugate scalar nodes in your model, very nearly replicating (with a few possible exceptions) the sampler assignments used by JAGS.

That said; it's not *all* about ESS.  The slice sampling will (generally) give higher ESS, but at the expense of a longer MCMC runtime.  We usually consider "MCMC efficiency" (which we define as min(ESS) / runtime, where the min() is taken across the sampled parameters) as the metric of how well an MCMC is doing, because that truly reflects how large an ESS you can generate, per unit runtime of MCMC sampling (for the slowest mixing model parameter).

But anyway, give the slice samplers a try, and hopefully that will raise up the ESS values you're getting.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

here a couple of tips. A first tip would be to use the argument calculate = FALSE when using the nimbleModel() function, which will build the nimble models faster. By default, calculate is set to TRUE, meaning that nimble calculates all deterministic nodes and logProbability values when creating the model, and with large models this can eat up a good amount of time and memory.

Second, it may be helpful in this case to write Z and prob in a vectorized form; this should help in that the resulting model would have less nodes to handle (i.e. two vector nodes instead of 2xn scalar nodes).  To do so, you would need a user-defined distribution for the vectorized version of the Bernoulli variable, that takes a vector of probabilities and returns the total log-probability.  If you are not familiar with user-defined distributions, they are covered in Chapter 12.2 of the User Manual <https://r-nimble.org/manuals/NimbleUserManual.pdf>, plus there are a couple of examples using them in our examples page <https://r-nimble.org/examples> on the website ("Writing a new distribution" and the "stochastic volatility" ones). And of course, feel free to ask for clarifications here!

Anyway, I've modified your example including these two tips and been able to try it out on my laptop. Let me know how it works for you, or if something is unclear.

Best,

Sally

###############################
# Toy Example
library(nimble)

# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000
beta<-c(1,1)
XMat<-cbind(runif(n,-1,1),runif(n,-1,1))
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize
consts   <- list(n=n)
data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat)
inits    <- list(beta1=0,beta2=0)

# SP: user defined distribution
# for a vector of bernoulli variables

dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),
                 log  = integer(0, default = 1)) {

    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

# Model String

model_binary_string_conj <- nimbleCode({
    # Data Model

    # SP: vectorized version using a user defined distribution
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1 + exp(XB[1:n]))
    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])

XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]

    # Parameter Model
    beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
    beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})

Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string_conj,
                    data = data,
                    constants=consts,

                    inits = inits,
                    calculate = FALSE) ## this should help to reduce memory & time

cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)
RmodelConf$printSamplers()
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta1", "beta2"))
bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)

cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC, project = Rmodel)

# Run sampler
niter=1000
cMCMC$run(niter)

gsamples_extended <- as.matrix(cMCMC$mvSamples)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Let me chime in with a couple of notes.

It is more important for NIMBLE than for JAGS to provide sensible and complete inits.  If you are not doing that, it could explain some degree of worse performance of NIMBLE.  That could be one source of the slice sampler warnings you saw.

It is also important to recognize there are relatively simple special cases where JAGS is at its best relative to NIMBLE, and simple lms and glms may potentially be those cases, anecdotally.

-Perry

On Wed, Jun 24, 2020 at 2:56 PM MIke Sparago <mikes...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for your reply, Daniel.  I attended the recent NIMBLE workshop and recall the discussion about MCMC efficiency.  As far as a 'best practice', we have traditionally adopted the guidance found in Kruschke's book and blog, where he suggests an ESS of at least 10,000. Certainly, the diagnostics plots look convincing with multiple chains at that level of ESS, which helps to sell the approach to those less familiar Bayesian modeling.  I will take another look at MCMC efficiency as a metric going forward.
>
> Regarding your suggestion of using 'onlySlice = TRUE', I am in the process of testing, but am seeing Warnings for "slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions" for several parameters, with current parameter values on the order of 1E+16.  I will see if there is any improvement when the MCMC has completed.  Thanks again.
>
>
> On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 4:33:49 PM UTC-4, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > Mike, when you configure the MCMC, usually a step using configureMCMC(), you could try adding the option:
> > configureMCMC(model, onlySlice = TRUE)
> >
> > This will assign slice samplers for all non-conjugate scalar nodes in your model, very nearly replicating (with a few possible exceptions) the sampler assignments used by JAGS.
> >
> > That said; it's not *all* about ESS.  The slice sampling will (generally) give higher ESS, but at the expense of a longer MCMC runtime.  We usually consider "MCMC efficiency" (which we define as min(ESS) / runtime, where the min() is taken across the sampled parameters) as the metric of how well an MCMC is doing, because that truly reflects how large an ESS you can generate, per unit runtime of MCMC sampling (for the slowest mixing model parameter).

> Hi Ben,
>
> here a couple of tips. A first tip would be to use the argument calculate = FALSE when using the nimbleModel() function, which will build the nimble models faster. By default, calculate is set to TRUE, meaning that nimble calculates all deterministic nodes and logProbability values when creating the model, and with large models this can eat up a good amount of time and memory.
>
> Second, it may be helpful in this case to write Z and prob in a vectorized form; this should help in that the resulting model would have less nodes to handle (i.e. two vector nodes instead of 2xn scalar nodes).  To do so, you would need a user-defined distribution for the vectorized version of the Bernoulli variable, that takes a vector of probabilities and returns the total log-probability.  If you are not familiar with user-defined distributions, they are covered in Chapter 12.2 of the User Manual <https://r-nimble.org/manuals/NimbleUserManual.pdf>, plus there are a couple of examples using them in our examples page <https://r-nimble.org/examples> on the website ("Writing a new distribution" and the "stochastic volatility" ones). And of course, feel free to ask for clarifications here!
>
> Anyway, I've modified your example including these two tips and been able to try it out on my laptop. Let me know how it works for you, or if something is unclear.
>
> Best,
>
> Sally
>
>
> ###############################
> # Toy Example
> library(nimble)
>
> # Generate Binary Data
> n=1000000
> beta<-c(1,1)
> XMat<-cbind(runif(n,-1,1),runif(n,-1,1))
> linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
> prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
> z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)
>
> # Initialize
> consts   <- list(n=n)
> data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat)
> inits    <- list(beta1=0,beta2=0)
>
> # SP: user defined distribution
> # for a vector of bernoulli variables
>
> dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x    = double(1),
>                  prob = double(1),
>                  log  = integer(0, default = 1)) {
>
>     returnType(double(0))
>     logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
>     if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
>   }
> )
>
> # Model String
>
> model_binary_string_conj <- nimbleCode({
>     # Data Model
>
>     # SP: vectorized version using a user defined distribution
>     prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1 + exp(XB[1:n]))
>     Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])
>
>
>
> XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]
>
>     # Parameter Model
>     beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
>     beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
> })
>
>
> Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string_conj,
>                     data = data,
>                     constants=consts,
>                     inits = inits,
>                     calculate = FALSE) ## this should help to reduce memory & time
>
>
> cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
>
> RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)
> RmodelConf$printSamplers()
> RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta1", "beta2"))
> bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)
> cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC, project = Rmodel)
>
>

> gsamples_extended <- as.matrix(cMCMC$mvSamples)
>

messages.subject: EnKF + PMCMC for multivariate SSM
messages.subject_clean: EnKF + PMCMC for multivariate SSM
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to the developers and contributors for all the great work building this useful software.

I am interested in utilizing NIMBLE's ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) in a particle marginal Metropolis Hastings (PMMH) algorithm to fit a state space model (SSM) with unknown parameters. The SSM is multivariate, and the covariance matrix depends on unknown, time-varying parameters that I hope to estimate as part of the model fitting procedure. Finally, the evolutions of the state equation can be non-linear (although both the observation and evolution processes are conditionally Gaussian). As a reference, the model is an example of what Katzfuss, Stroud, and Wikle (2020) call a hierarchical SSM, but with no transformation layer (eqs. 2-4 in their paper).

So far, I've been successful using NIMBLE to create particle filters for my model with fixed parameters, and as I had hoped the EnKF seems to perform better than the bootstrap particle filter. I've taken a swing at the full PMMF with the help of the recent paper by Michaud et al. on arXiv, soon to be published in JSS, but I've hit some snags. Rather than post a MWE, I wanted to start by trying to clarify a few things, and ask whether there might be any existing examples of similar applications that I could use as a guide. (1) From what I read in Section 6.1 of Michaud et al. (2017), it sounds like NIMBLE's PMMH approaches are limited to bootstrap and auxiliary particle filters, and so using an EnKF requires a little extra work (i.e., I can't just create the EnKF using buildEnsembleKF() and then set the control argument pf = EnKF). Is that correct? If so, could you help me understand what steps would be necessary to connect these two pieces in NIMBLE? (2) After a little trial and error, it appears to me that to use a multivariate EnKF, both the latent state vector and the observation vector must be specified as coming from a multivariate Gaussian distribution in the model code. My observation vector is conditionally independent given the latent states (i.e., the covariance for the observation process is diagonal). Is there any way to make use of the conditional independence at the observation level to gain some computational efficiency?

Thanks for your help,
Henry Scharf

Katzfuss, M., Stroud, J. R., & Wikle, C. K. (2020). Ensemble Kalman methods for high-dimensional hierarchical dynamic space-time models. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 115(530), 866-885.

Michaud, N., de Valpine, P., Turek, D., Paciorek, C. J., & Nguyen, D. (2017). Sequential Monte Carlo methods in the nimble R package. arXiv preprint arXiv:1703.06206.

Daniel / Perry,

We appear to have resolved the problem, with your help of course.  After I responded to Perry's post, where I indicated that a large proportion of our data is censored, it occurred to me that the censoring vector (from dinterval) was treated as data, as opposed to constants.  Moving the censoring vector to constants brought the ESS much closer to JAGS.  Once that was completed, blocking improvements were also more successful.  Additionally, we saw ESS improvements when providing a better initial value for one parameter.  As Perry indicated, the slice sampler warnings disappeared after the initial value was improved for that parameter.

Daniel's suggestion to use 'onlySlice = TRUE' did indeed increase the ESS,  but significantly increased the runtime, as expected.

I feel like we have a good starting point now, and can work toward further MCMC improvements.

Thanks, Mike

> >

To do so, you would need a user-defined distribution for the vectorized version of the Bernoulli variable, that takes a vector of probabilities and returns the total log-probability.  If you are not familiar with user-defined distributions, they are covered in Chapter 12.2 of the User Manual <https://r-nimble.org/manuals/NimbleUserManual.pdf>, plus there are a couple of examples using them in our examples page <https://r-nimble.org/examples> on the website ("Writing a new distribution" and the "stochastic volatility" ones). > >     # Data Model

messages.subject: Some Interactions between Nimble and R not working in parallel
messages.subject_clean: Some Interactions between Nimble and R not working in parallel
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I usually run my nimble models in parallel using the doparallel package and foreach. Typically, this works quite well and since I often run 3 chains it results in a speedup of between 2-3 times. However, as I have started to code more complex models I have run into issues running in parallel. For some reason there are certain interactions between R and Nimble that do not work properly in parallel and I do not understand why.

The main example I have involves removing and adding samplers to several nodes. I use the following for loop which works when not in parallel.

for(loc in 1:160){

dq <- !mainmodel$isData(paste0("S[",loc,", ]"))
mainmodelConf$removeSampler(paste0("S[",loc,", dq]"))
mainmodelConf$addSampler(target = mainmodel$expandNodeNames(paste0("S[",loc,", dq]")),
                        type = "my_sampler")

}

S is a two dimensional node S[1:160,1:85]. Some of S is data and some needs to be sampled. The idea here is that S[loc,dq] are S nodes in location loc that are not data and need to be sampled. I remove the default nimble sampler and then add my own sampler. This works when not in parallel.

In parallel however it does not work. dq is created correctly as a logical vector but nimble is unable to understand what S[loc,dq] is and print(mainmodel$expandNodeNames(paste0("S[",loc,", dq]"))) returns an empty vector.

Anyone understand why some things work when not in parallel but do not work when in parallel and how to fix it?

Hi Chris,

I created a very simple example that shows the issue

library(nimble)
library(parallel)

S <- rep(NA,10)
S[c(2,4,6,8)] <- 0
#some S data and some not

mainCode <- nimbleCode({

  for(i in 1:10){
    S[i] ~ dbern(.5)
  }

}
)

myData <- list(S=S)
myInits <- list(S=rep(1,10))

mainModel <- nimbleModel(code=mainCode,data = myData,inits = myInits)

mainModel$S

dq <- !mainModel$isData("S[]")
mainModel$expandNodeNames("S[dq]")

#so it works here

parrallel_nimble <- function(X,data,inits){

  library(nimble)

  mainCode <- nimbleCode({

    for(i in 1:10){
      S[i] ~ dbern(.5)
    }

  }
  )

  mainModel <- nimbleModel(code=mainCode,data = data,inits = inits)

  dq <- !mainModel$isData("S[]")

  return(mainModel$expandNodeNames("S[dq]"))

}

parrallel_nimble(X=1:3,data=myData,inits=myInits)

#works again

this_cluster <- makeCluster(3)

fit_par <- parLapply(cl = this_cluster,X = 1:3,
                     fun = parrallel_nimble,
                     data=myData,inits=myInits)

fit_par[[1]]
#just empty character vector

stopCluster(this_cluster)

Hi Sally,

Thank you very much for the clarification. The error no longer comes up now, so feel free to disregard.

Using your suggestion (set calculate=FALSE and vectorizing operations), I was able to bring down the model building and compilation wall times for the case when n=1e+06 and k=2. Now, I have increased the # of predictors from k=2 to k=150 while keeping n=1e+06. This has taken 2.5 hours to build the model using nimbleModel() and I am still waiting for the sampler to compile (been 6 hours so far). Are these walltimes typical of such cases?

Code for a toy example (similar to my actual application) is as follows.

#Toy Example
# Generate Binary Data

n=1000000 ; k=200
beta<-rep(1,k)
XMat<-matrix(rnorm(n*k),nrow=n,ncol=k)

linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize

consts   <- list(n=n,k=k)
data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat, mn=rep(0,k),pCov=100*diag(k))
inits    <- list(beta=rep(0,k))

# for a vector of bernoulli variables
dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),
                 log  = integer(0, default = 1)) {

    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

# Model String

model_binary_string <- nimbleCode({
  # Data Model

    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1+exp(XB[1:n]))

    XB[1:n]<-X[1:n,1:k]%*%beta[1:k]

  # Parameter Model
  beta[1:k] ~    dmnorm(mean = mn[1:k], cov = pCov[1:k,1:k])
})

# Build Model
Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string, data = data,

                    constants=consts, inits = inits,calculate = FALSE)

cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)

RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta"))

bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC)

Best,
Ben

messages.subject: Re: Compilation difficulties using nimbleFunctionList for meta-population data structure
messages.subject_clean: Compilation difficulties using nimbleFunctionList for meta-population data structure
messages.body_plain:
David, it's good to hear from you, and I'm glad you're still moving forward with SIR models in NIMBLE.  I took a look at your code.  There were 2 things not working for you.

(1) In order to access compiled nimbleFunctionLists, and elements within them, and methods within them (including the run method), and the same goes for variables and methods within compiled objects in general, you'll need to set the nimble system option:

nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)

This will allow accessing methods, variables, etc, internal to *compiled* nimbleFunctions, for example:

cStates$StatesInPopList[[1]]$run() # DT: works

Without setting that nimble system option, it's still possible to "dig into" nested compiled objects - it's just more unwieldy and unintuitive.  If that becomes a priority, since compilation will be somewhat slower after setting this option, then take a look in the User Manual (section 15.4.10 it looks like) and search for "valueInCompiledNimbleFunction".

I added this option to your code (modified), which is attached.

(2) The other thing that wasn't working for you - NIMBLE isn't quite always as general as we might hope, or it might seem.  In this case, access to arbitrary elements of the nested nimbleFuntionList object (StatesInPopList) isn't available as "random access" as we might like.  That is, I don't think you can just pass in a **run-time** argument ("pop"), and then access *only* the pop-th element in the list (that is, StatesInPopList[pop] ).

Instead, I think you'll always have to iterate over the entire list as:
for(i in 1:nPops) {     ## DT
    ... arbitrary code involving: StatesInPopList[[i]]
}

So, just a little careful thinking will get around this problem, although I admit it's a "work-around".  See the modified script attached, where I just added a conditional check inside this loop, for whether (i == pop) on each loop iteration.

Anyway, I think the modified script, attached, should get you working.  Like I said, you could find some performance gains from *not* using the nimble option mentioned above; or, if the "looping" I introduced becomes a problem (which I hope might not happen), then we could talk about other options there, also.

Keep at it!

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Bessel I function for Von Mises distribution
messages.subject_clean: Bessel I function for Von Mises distribution
messages.body_plain:
Solved -- we set up a nimbleExternalCall for the C version of bessel I called by R's besselI() function (instead of the one from the GNU Library). The function is available in the Rmath library (Rmath.h file, search "bessel_i").

The nimbleExternalCall i set up as follows:

sink('besselI.h')

cat('
extern "C" {
 double bessel_I_internal(double x, double alpha,  double expo);
}
')

sink()

sink('besselI.cpp')

cat('
 #include <Rmath.h>
 #include "besselI.h"
 double bessel_I_internal(double x, double alpha, double expo) {
   double ans = Rf_bessel_i(x, alpha, expo);
   return(ans);
 }
')

sink()

system2("R", c("CMD", "SHLIB", "besselI.cpp")) ## Ignore the .so (or .DLL).  We will use the besselI.o

RbesselI <- nimbleExternalCall(function(x = double(), alpha = double(), expo = double()){},
                               Cfun =  'bessel_I_internal',
                               headerFile = 'besselI.h', ## see note about paths belos
                               returnType = double(),
                               oFile = 'besselI.o')

## Check if it works by compiling it as a stand-alone nimbleFunction
cRbesselI <- compileNimble(RbesselI, dirName = ".")

cRbesselI(3, -.2, 2) ## According to besselI source code, the besselI C function in Rmath uses 1 = FALSE, 2 = TRUE in the last argument
besselI(3, -.2, TRUE) ## Matches above

## Write a nimbleFunction to wrap call to RbesselI for use in a model
besselI_in_model <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(), alpha = double(), expo = double()) {
    ans <- RbesselI(x, alpha, 1 + (expo != 0)) ## handling of expo mimics besselI in R
    return(ans)
    returnType(double())
  })

## Use it in a model
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
  x ~ dunif(0, 10)
  nu ~ dunif(-1, 0)
  z <- besselI_in_model(x, nu, expo = TRUE)
})

demoModel <- nimbleModel(demoCode, inits = list(x = 3, nu = -.2),
                         check = FALSE, calculate = FALSE) ## Can't calculate in R with a nimbleExternalCall

CdemoModel <- compileNimble(demoModel, dirName = ".")

CdemoModel$z
CdemoModel$calculate("z")
CdemoModel$z

## A note about paths.  I recommend something like headerFile = normalizePath(file.path(getwd(), 'besselI.h'))
##  and similar for oFile.
## This is important when compiling the model, which is not by default done in your local directory.
## An alternative, which I've used above, is to give local paths to hearderFile and oFile
##   and then use dirName = "." in compileNimble for the model, which makes it use your local directory
##   for the C++ files.
## On my system, this avoided problems with a space in getwd() due to "Google Drive", but those are
##   just OS details.

Thanks a lot for your help with this, Perry!

Simona

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for the reproducible example. I tested this and indeed it is scaling poorly, both in terms of memory use and in terms of time to set up the model and MCMC. Your X matrix is 1.2 GB if k=150, but that doesn't explain the memory use I'm seeing. And once you've vectorized, there are very few nodes in the model, which would usually make setting up the model and MCMC go much faster than the setup time that we're seeing here.

We'll have to do a deeper dive to really understand what is going on. We'll be in touch once we know more.

Chris

Hi Chris,

Thank you very much for your response, and I appreciate you taking a look at this. We have been using nimble to fit these types of high-dimensional models to much success. However,  we recently began experiencing these scaling issues, particularly with larger datasets (n>100k).

In our actual application, we have n=2.4 million binary data points and a dense design matrix X that is n x 150. We modified the code using Sally's suggestions. For a n=180k example, it took 16 minutes to compile the sampler and 2 minutes to generate 1k samples via the MCMC algorithm.

Best,
Ben

hi Ben,

That's quite helpful (and encouraging) to know that this is a recent change.

1) What version of nimble are you using now, and if you know or can
easily figure it out, what version were you using before you started
experiencing the scaling issues?

2) When you were getting good performance before, what was the largest
'n' and 'k' where things were working ok? Also, was the model
fundamentally similar to the example you provided in this thread?

My hope is that we can revert the problematic behavior to get you back
to where things were and then if you apply Sally's suggestions, things
will be better than they were before.

Chris

Hi Chris,

My apologies. Unfortunately, I need to backtrack on one of my statements. I have not been able to run the example code (n=1 million and k=150) successfully. What I meant to say is that I recently started modeling large datasets (n = 100k to 1 million) using nimble; hence, I recently ran into scaling issues due to the larger datasets. In the past, my datasets were limited to ~20k observations. Since nimble compiled and ran the MCMC algorithm quickly for these "smaller"  n=20k datasets, I assumed scalability wouldn't be an issue.

As per your questions:
1. I am using nimble version 0.9.0 on both my laptop and the cluster. I believe this may be the only version that I have used so far.
2. The largest n and k I have used is n=270k and k=153. This required 31 minutes to compile the sampler and 6 hours to run 100k iterations of the MCMC algorithm. My true model is fundamentally similar to the one I provided (with some modifications). I can send you the actual code directly.

Sorry about the miscommunication earlier. Please let me know if you need anything else from my end. Thank you so much!

Best,
Ben

Hi David and Daniel,

I took a look at this.  There is an easier workaround to the indexing issue.

First, the warnings about needing to define pop before compilation are misfires of the static code processing that tries to give helpful tips.  We'll have to fix that, but you can ignore it.

Second, the problem using pop as the index arises only for

StatesInPopList[[pop]]$run(), not for the other method calls.

An easier workaround than Daniel's is simply
i <- pop
StatesInPopList[[i]]$run()

A brief explanation:
nimble does name-mangling of arguments.  For example, "pop" will become "ARG1_pop_".  This makes it possible to support the use of "log" as an argument name.  In R, even the name of a base R function like log can be re-used, and it commonly is in distribution functions that take "log = TRUE".  In C++, one can't use a language keyword like log as an argument name, so we mangle argument names to avoid that conflict.  However that means that we need to replace "pop" everywhere with "ARG1_pop_".  Evidently that is not working for "StatesInPopList[[pop]]$run()", which can be seen by inspection of the generated C++ (not something most people want to do, I know!).  Given that it works for the other method calls, this case where it fails must be due to some quirky oversight or corner case.  In the workaround, the name mangling replacement works for the simple "i <- pop" and then "i" works in "StatesInPopList[[i]]$run()"

Attached is the simpler version that works.

Thanks again for turning up these issues.  I'll file two bugs arising from this.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

There are several reasons nimble encounters scaling issues.  For any model variable, nimble needs to allow for complete generality of how nodes may be declared in arbitrary ways for indexed subsets of a variable and how arbitrary subsets of it (not necessarily corresponding to declared nodes) may be used as arguments for other declarations.  nimble then needs to make a graph from all that generality.  This leads to a fair bit of bookkeeping.  There are some ways to improve this that we have on our agenda, and one of them is currently lined up in a pull request on github.  Some of the issues that arise have to do with R scaling issues for the steps we implement in R.  There are deeper ways to envision better scaling, but they will be longer term.

Back to your needs: Here is a way to work around some of nimble's scaling issues.  You can use nimbleRcall to keep large constant objects entirely out of the model.  In the example below, I have kept X and pCov out of the model.  In effect, nimble is still managing the model graph and using its MCMC system, but some of the big calculations are thrown back to R.  There will be some overhead from going back to R, but maybe those costs won't be too bad compared to the cost of the large calculations.  Of course, I don't know if you want to expand the model to have X and/or pCov be non-constant, but if so you can build on the basic scheme shown below.  It would also be possible to have the large objects like X and pCov be in C++ objects used by C++ functions via nimbleExternalCall, but that would take some direct C++ coding.

With the code below, everything builds reasonably quickly.

library(nimble)

#Toy Example
# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000 ; k=200

#n <- 100000; k <- 100 # smaller case Perry used for prototyping

beta<-rep(1,k)
XMat<-matrix(rnorm(n*k),nrow=n,ncol=k)
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize

keepInR <- list(X=XMat, pCov=100*diag(k))
consts   <- list(n=n,k=k)
data     <- list(Z=z, mn=rep(0,k))

inits    <- list(beta=rep(0,k))

# for a vector of bernoulli variables
dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),

                 log  = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero

    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

## Use R's lexical scoping to create R functions to be called
## via nimbleRcall that will find large objects like
## X and pCov in their enclosing environment.
makeRfuns <- function(keepInR) {
  X <- keepInR$X
  pCov <- keepInR$pCov
  chol_pCov <- chol(pCov)
  RcalculateXB <- function(beta) {
    as.numeric(X %*% beta)
  }
  dRdmnorm <- function(x, mean, log) {
    nimble::dmnorm_chol(x, mean, cholesky = chol_pCov, prec_param = FALSE, log = log)
  }
  list(RcalculateXB = RcalculateXB, dRdmnorm = dRdmnorm)
}

## Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
Rfuns <- makeRfuns(keepInR)
RcalculateXB_internal <- Rfuns$RcalculateXB ## I think these need to be in .GlobalEnv
dRdmnorm_internal <- Rfuns$dRdmnorm

## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R functions.
RcalculateXB <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(1)) {}, returnType = double(1), Rfun = 'RcalculateXB_internal')
dRdmnorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(1), mean = double(1), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {}, returnType = double(), Rfun = 'dRdmnorm_internal')

## Write the model using the nimbleRcalls.  Note that X and pCov do not appear in the model.

# Model String
model_binary_string <- nimbleCode({
  # Data Model
    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1+exp(XB[1:n]))

    XB[1:n] <- RcalculateXB(beta[1:k])

  # Parameter Model
  beta[1:k] ~ dRdmnorm(mean = mn[1:k])

})

# Build Model
Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string, data = data,
                    constants=consts, inits = inits,calculate = FALSE)

system.time(cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel))
system.time(RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)) ## could use useConjugacy=FALSE
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta"))
system.time(bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf))
system.time(cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC))
system.time(cMCMC$run(10))
