messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for the message.  Let me start by pointing you here to see if you've updated nimble and covered your bases on R 4.0 issues: https://r-nimble.org/download  There were some changes in R 4.0 that necessitated nimble 0.9.1 and attention to Rtools installation changes.

Please send another message if you can't resolve it from the information there.

-Perry

>

messages.subject: Large memory demands by WAIC calculation
messages.subject_clean: Large memory demands by WAIC calculation
messages.body_plain:
I've been noticing pretty large memory demands when calculating WAIC for a model I've been fitting. I'm currently running many models in parallel in an Azure VM. Memory spikes up during the WAIC calculation, so I presume that it is the cause.

I'm fitting hurdle-negative binomial models on about 7k data points (so a lot). With 30,000 iterations and 3 chains, I'm getting memory requirements of about 5-6 GB of memory usage for a single model during the WAIC calculation step.

I was considering opening a GitHub issue but figured this would be a better place to start an informal discussion to see if an issue is warranted.

Thanks for any insight!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

Thank you very much for looking into this for me and explaining why we experience scaling issues, particularly when interfacing with R. I've taken your suggestion and used the nimbleRcall() to keep large fixed matrices out of the nimble model. I've kept the massive design matrix X in R using nimbleRcall(), and this seems to have done the trick. The model builds quickly and the sampler runs faster than before. I've scaled this up to a larger dataset (n>2.5 million) with p=150 covariates, and I am able to build the model within 2 minutes (as opposed to 6 hours previously). The mcmc sampler also runs 1.5 times faster than before. This is great!

Again, thank you for providing the code. I will most likely build upon it for cases when I need to vary the design matrix X or pCov.

Best,
Ben

On Friday, June 26, 2020 at 2:59:30 PM UTC-4 pdevalpine wrote:
> Hi Ben,
>
> There are several reasons nimble encounters scaling issues.  For any model variable, nimble needs to allow for complete generality of how nodes may be declared in arbitrary ways for indexed subsets of a variable and how arbitrary subsets of it (not necessarily corresponding to declared nodes) may be used as arguments for other declarations.  nimble then needs to make a graph from all that generality.  This leads to a fair bit of bookkeeping.  There are some ways to improve this that we have on our agenda, and one of them is currently lined up in a pull request on github.  Some of the issues that arise have to do with R scaling issues for the steps we implement in R.  There are deeper ways to envision better scaling, but they will be longer term.
>
> Back to your needs: Here is a way to work around some of nimble's scaling issues.  You can use nimbleRcall to keep large constant objects entirely out of the model.  In the example below, I have kept X and pCov out of the model.  In effect, nimble is still managing the model graph and using its MCMC system, but some of the big calculations are thrown back to R.  There will be some overhead from going back to R, but maybe those costs won't be too bad compared to the cost of the large calculations.  Of course, I don't know if you want to expand the model to have X and/or pCov be non-constant, but if so you can build on the basic scheme shown below.  It would also be possible to have the large objects like X and pCov be in C++ objects used by C++ functions via nimbleExternalCall, but that would take some direct C++ coding.
>
> With the code below, everything builds reasonably quickly.
>
> library(nimble)
>
>
> #Toy Example
> # Generate Binary Data
> n=1000000 ; k=200
> #n <- 100000; k <- 100 # smaller case Perry used for prototyping
>
> beta<-rep(1,k)
> XMat<-matrix(rnorm(n*k),nrow=n,ncol=k)
> linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
> prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
> z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)
>
> # Initialize
> keepInR <- list(X=XMat, pCov=100*diag(k))
> consts   <- list(n=n,k=k)
> data     <- list(Z=z, mn=rep(0,k))
>
> inits    <- list(beta=rep(0,k))
>
> # for a vector of bernoulli variables
> dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x    = double(1),
>                  prob = double(1),
>                  log  = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero
>
>
>     returnType(double(0))
>     logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
>     if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
>   }
> )
>
> ## Use R's lexical scoping to create R functions to be called
> ## via nimbleRcall that will find large objects like
> ## X and pCov in their enclosing environment.
> makeRfuns <- function(keepInR) {
>   X <- keepInR$X
>   pCov <- keepInR$pCov
>   chol_pCov <- chol(pCov)
>   RcalculateXB <- function(beta) {
>     as.numeric(X %*% beta)
>   }
>   dRdmnorm <- function(x, mean, log) {
>     nimble::dmnorm_chol(x, mean, cholesky = chol_pCov, prec_param = FALSE, log = log)
>   }
>   list(RcalculateXB = RcalculateXB, dRdmnorm = dRdmnorm)
> }
>
> ## Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
> Rfuns <- makeRfuns(keepInR)
> RcalculateXB_internal <- Rfuns$RcalculateXB ## I think these need to be in .GlobalEnv
> dRdmnorm_internal <- Rfuns$dRdmnorm
>
> ## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R functions.
> RcalculateXB <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(1)) {}, returnType = double(1), Rfun = 'RcalculateXB_internal')
> dRdmnorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(1), mean = double(1), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {}, returnType = double(), Rfun = 'dRdmnorm_internal')
>
> ## Write the model using the nimbleRcalls.  Note that X and pCov do not appear in the model.
>
> # Model String
> model_binary_string <- nimbleCode({
>   # Data Model
>     Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])
>     prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1+exp(XB[1:n]))
>     XB[1:n] <- RcalculateXB(beta[1:k])
>
>   # Parameter Model
>   beta[1:k] ~ dRdmnorm(mean = mn[1:k])
>
> })
>
>
> # Build Model
> Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string, data = data,
>                     constants=consts, inits = inits,calculate = FALSE)
> system.time(cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel))
> system.time(RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)) ## could use useConjugacy=FALSE
> RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta"))
> system.time(bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf))
> system.time(cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC))
> system.time(cMCMC$run(10))
>
>

messages.subject_clean: Alternative to saving mcmc samples as R matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Let's say your compiled mcmc is called cmcmc.

If by pulling the samples into R, you mean the common step of "as.matrix(cmcmc$mvSamples)", yes, you can take more fine-grained control over that.  If instead you are using either nimbleMCMC or creating cmcmc and then using runMCMC(cmcmc,...), you will instead need to call cmcmc$run(...) yourself so you can take control of retrieving the samples.

The object cmcmc$mvSamples is what we call a compiled modelValues object.  Please check out Chapter 14 of the User Manual to see how you can access its contents in more or less natural R style, like cmcmc$mvSamples[["beta"]].  There is also concise information in help(modelValuesBaseClass), as directed from help(modelValues).

You might also find the monitors2 and thin2 system helpful, if you can get by with smaller samples (more thinning) for some of your variables.

Responses will be slow for a few days.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk, this looks like an issue that is not directly related to parallelization, as you figured out.

1) The argument to expandNodeNames should be a character vector that provides a valid node (e.g., "S[3]") or nodes (e.g., "S[2:4]") or a valid variable (e.g. "S"). So in your case "S[dq1]" is not valid because there is no node named "S[dq1]", only nodes named "S[1]", "S[2]", etc.

Here's what you need to do -- evaluate `dq1` and use the result to create a valid node name:

  dq1 <- !Model$isData("S[]")

  nodeName <- paste0('S[', dq1, ']')
  return(Model$expandNodeNames(nodeName))

2) It's actually an "accident" that what you tried to do worked in any context. Basically, within our processing when we try to determine the set of nodes
that the user has passed in, we actually allow `dq1` to be evaluated when we should really error out.
In some of your cases, R is able to find `dq1` via R's scoping rules and in other cases it is not. When it can't find `dq1`, it returns the error you see.
So it's not surprising that you encountered this in the context of parallelization, where it becomes more complicated to find R variables.

3) We've encountered this issue in other contexts, but I haven't had the time yet to put in better error trapping such that all cases where you
tried to use "S[dq1]" would error out with an error message that would be easy for you to interpret.

Please try the change above, and if you notice any further parallelization issues, let us know.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: EnKF + PMCMC for multivariate SSM
messages.subject_clean: EnKF + PMCMC for multivariate SSM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henry, this raises a number of interesting questions. Here goes...

1) You cannot directly use the output of buildEnsembleKF and set pf = EnKF.  The reason is that our particle MCMC requires that the particle filter that it uses must have methods to get and set the last log-likelihood and have access to the mvEWsamples data structure. (For the latter issue, it might simply be a matter of renaming the 'mvSamples' in our ensemble KF to be 'mvEWsamples'.) If you look in the code for sampler_RW_PF or sampler_RW_PF_block in our MCMC_samplers.R file you should be able to see how these are used in the context of the particle MCMC.

1a) I presume one can get an estimate of the log marginal likelihood  from the ensemble KF or you wouldn't be asking your question, though I'd have to refresh my memory of the algorithm to know how one uses the ensemble KF to estimate the marginal likelihood.

1b) I haven't thought about it carefully, but I'm optimistic that you could take our ensemble KF code (in filtering_enkf.R) and modify it so it has the parts that are needed to use it with our sampler_RW_PF or sampler_RW_PF_block. We'd be happy to answer questions and iterate with you if you wanted to take that on as a project.

2) As far as what kinds of distributions are allowed, I see our documentation for the ensemble KF could be improved. If you look in enkfScalFunc and enkfMultFunc, you see we expect the distribution to have 'mean' and either 'var' or 'cov' respectively. And if you look in ENKFStep, you'll see that we expect the 'cov' to be a matrix when we create 'kMat'.

2a) If you specify the observations as having a dmnorm distribution and provide "cov" (rather than "prec" or "cholesky") then when the enKF goes to get the "cov" of the observations in getVar() using getParam(), it will just be a direct copy of "cov" out of the model without any matrix algebra involved. So it's a bit inefficient in that the zeroes are copied and then when 'kMat' is created, one is also adding those 0s on the off-diagonal. But it's probably not too much of a cost compared to all the other calculations going on. However, if you need/want to parameterize the dmnorm for your observations using "prec" or "cholesky" rather than "cov" , then under the hood nimble will need to do matrix algebra to construct "cov" and that would be costly if done repeatedly, such as if the "prec" or "cholesky" were functions of unknown parameters. Of course you are probably needing to construct "cov" from scalar variance parameters. It's probably most efficient to do this in a user-defined function, but doing it as a for  loop in the model code directly may not be too inefficient if the length of the vector at each time point is not too long.

2b) It shouldn't be too hard to modify our enKF to handle other observation distributions. E.g., you could write your own dmnorm_diagonal distribution that is parameterized in terms of a vector of variances. Then in the enKF, you could modify the line for creating 'kMat' so that it takes advantage of the fact that the covariance is diagonal and just uses the vector of variances appropriately.  You'd need to modify the 'returnType' of 'getVar' to be one-dimensional.

Final note: we are in the process of pulling our particle filters out of the main nimble package and into a new package called 'nimbleSMC'. If you dove into this and modified our enKF in ways that would be useful for others, we'd be happy to discuss if it made sense to add your new functionality to that package, with you being a co-author of the package then, of course.

-chris

> Many thanks to the developers and contributors for all the great work building this useful software.
>
> I am interested in utilizing NIMBLE's ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) in a particle marginal Metropolis Hastings (PMMH) algorithm to fit a state space model (SSM) with unknown parameters. The SSM is multivariate, and the covariance matrix depends on unknown, time-varying parameters that I hope to estimate as part of the model fitting procedure. Finally, the evolutions of the state equation can be non-linear (although both the observation and evolution processes are conditionally Gaussian). As a reference, the model is an example of what Katzfuss, Stroud, and Wikle (2020) call a hierarchical SSM, but with no transformation layer (eqs. 2-4 in their paper).
>
> So far, I've been successful using NIMBLE to create particle filters for my model with fixed parameters, and as I had hoped the EnKF seems to perform better than the bootstrap particle filter. I've taken a swing at the full PMMF with the help of the recent paper by Michaud et al. on arXiv, soon to be published in JSS, but I've hit some snags. Rather than post a MWE, I wanted to start by trying to clarify a few things, and ask whether there might be any existing examples of similar applications that I could use as a guide. (1) From what I read in Section 6.1 of Michaud et al. (2017), it sounds like NIMBLE's PMMH approaches are limited to bootstrap and auxiliary particle filters, and so using an EnKF requires a little extra work (i.e., I can't just create the EnKF using buildEnsembleKF() and then set the control argument pf = EnKF). Is that correct? If so, could you help me understand what steps would be necessary to connect these two pieces in NIMBLE? My observation vector is conditionally independent given the latent states (i.e., the covariance for the observation process is diagonal). Is there any way to make use of the conditional independence at the observation level to gain some computational efficiency?
>
> Thanks for your help,
> Henry Scharf
>
>

Dear NIMBLE authors,

I got a question about the speed of execution.

a) In test.R (for an item response theory model), I compare two methods-- one uses 'no nimbleFunction' (see Line 23-31) and the other uses nimbleFunction (see Line 34). Why using nimbleFunction made execution slower? Can we speed it up by any tricks?

b) Line 34 is simply an intermediate computation. Can we avoid this to speed up the execution?

Thank you in advance, and thanks a lot for developing this great MCMC software.

Keith

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk, a few thoughts here:

1) You should definitely switch to

nodeName <- paste0('S[', dq1, ']')

Relying on the current syntax is not guaranteed to work in future versions of nimble.

2) It looks like there are some scoping issues with finding your user-defined sampler.

a) Please define the sampler within your parallelization function as you are doing for the model, MCMC configuration, etc.

Then add this line within your parallelization function:

assign('my_sampler', my_sampler, envir = .GlobalEnv)

The reason this is needed is that nimble is looking in R's global environment for the user defined sampler, but that sampler is being set up inside the parallelization function. I'm going to file an issue for one of the developers to see if we should modify how user-defined samplers are found.

b) I don't recommend defining the sampler in your main R session as it's a bit tricky to use clusterExport to get the sampler sent out to the workers because nimbleFunctions are more complicated than regular R objects. But I'll make a note that we should look into how to make this easier.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Large memory demands by WAIC calculation
messages.subject_clean: Large memory demands by WAIC calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

In calculating WAIC (which involves calculating predictive density values) we fill a matrix with a row for each MCMC sample and a column for each data point. With the number of iterations you have and the number of data points, this can use a lot of memory.

I doubt you need to save that many iterations to get a good posterior summary or a robust WAIC estimate, so you might want to thin your MCMC output to save on memory in this case, if you are running out of memory.

I believe we could modify our WAIC calculation to not store all those predictive density values at the same time, but it would be a bit involved because the current calculation tries to be careful about avoiding numerical underflow to ensure numerical stability. There are lots of models with as much or more data as you have, so we should try to make the WAIC work such that it doesn't use up so much memory. I'll make a note for us to look into this, though it's not something we'll likely get to in the very near term.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
I attempted to confirm that the dinterval() censored data vector should be treated as constants vs. data, since we (apparently) got higher ESS when making that change. I ran our model, which has a large proportion of censored data 10 times and calculated the min efficiency for both cases. These results (shown below) indicate that there is no significant difference in efficiency with the censoring vector as constants vs. data. I would have to retrace our steps again, but perhaps we had a change in initial values that caused our ESS improvement. We are currently close in ESS between JAGS and NIMBLE, but as you can see the MCMC efficiency is low.

Censoring Vector as Constants:

[1] 0.260  0.337  0.356  0.227  0.134  0.114  0.307  0.348  0.303  0.130

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.

 0.1140  0.1548  0.2821  0.2516  0.3298  0.3569

Censoring Vector as Data:

[1] 0.147  0.362  0.262  0.306  0.168  0.183  0.333  0.265  0.360  0.317

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.

 0.1472  0.2030  0.2857  0.2707  0.3293  0.3627

On Thursday, June 25, 2020 at 10:30:04 AM UTC-4, MIke Sparago wrote:
> Daniel / Perry,
>
> We appear to have resolved the problem, with your help of course.  After I responded to Perry's post, where I indicated that a large proportion of our data is censored, it occurred to me that the censoring vector (from dinterval) was treated as data, as opposed to constants.  Moving the censoring vector to constants brought the ESS much closer to JAGS.  Once that was completed, blocking improvements were also more successful.  Additionally, we saw ESS improvements when providing a better initial value for one parameter.  As Perry indicated, the slice sampler warnings disappeared after the initial value was improved for that parameter.
>
> Daniel's suggestion to use 'onlySlice = TRUE' did indeed increase the ESS,  but significantly increased the runtime, as expected.
>
> I feel like we have a good starting point now, and can work toward further MCMC improvements.
>
> Thanks, Mike
>
> On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 8:33:09 PM UTC-4, MIke Sparago wrote:
> > Thanks for the chime, Perry. My model is fully initialized and I am using the same initialization function with both NIMBLE and JAGS. Still, I will review the initial values, as you suggested.
> >
> > I was thinking of posting a minimal example, but would need to simplify the model before doing so. Although it is not as advanced as some of your ecological models, I do not consider it a simple GLM, with 1,305 observed stochastic nodes, 2,430 unobserved stochastic nodes and a graph size of 35.564. Perhaps the real answer is that we need to work on the parameterization.
> >
> > We are working with NIMBLE because there are opportunities with user-defined distributions that we need to explore, so we're not ready to give up yet.
> >
> > On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 7:42:28 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > Hi Mike,
> > >
> > > Let me chime in with a couple of notes.
> > >
> > > It is more important for NIMBLE than for JAGS to provide sensible and complete inits.  If you are not doing that, it could explain some degree of worse performance of NIMBLE.  That could be one source of the slice sampler warnings you saw.
> > >
> > > It is also important to recognize there are relatively simple special cases where JAGS is at its best relative to NIMBLE, and simple lms and glms may potentially be those cases, anecdotally.
> > >
> > > -Perry
> > >
> > > On Wed, Jun 24, 2020 at 2:56 PM MIke Sparago <mikes...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thanks for your reply, Daniel.  I attended the recent NIMBLE workshop and recall the discussion about MCMC efficiency.  As far as a 'best practice', we have traditionally adopted the guidance found in Kruschke's book and blog, where he suggests an ESS of at least 10,000. Certainly, the diagnostics plots look convincing with multiple chains at that level of ESS, which helps to sell the approach to those less familiar Bayesian modeling.  I will take another look at MCMC efficiency as a metric going forward.
> > > >
> > > > Regarding your suggestion of using 'onlySlice = TRUE', I am in the process of testing, but am seeing Warnings for "slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions" for several parameters, with current parameter values on the order of 1E+16.  I will see if there is any improvement when the MCMC has completed.  Thanks again.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Wednesday, June 24, 2020 at 4:33:49 PM UTC-4, Daniel Turek wrote:
> > > > > Mike, when you configure the MCMC, usually a step using configureMCMC(), you could try adding the option:
> > > > > configureMCMC(model, onlySlice = TRUE)
> > > > >
> > > > > This will assign slice samplers for all non-conjugate scalar nodes in your model, very nearly replicating (with a few possible exceptions) the sampler assignments used by JAGS.
> > > > >
> > > > > That said; it's not *all* about ESS.  The slice sampling will (generally) give higher ESS, but at the expense of a longer MCMC runtime.  We usually consider "MCMC efficiency" (which we define as min(ESS) / runtime, where the min() is taken across the sampled parameters) as the metric of how well an MCMC is doing, because that truly reflects how large an ESS you can generate, per unit runtime of MCMC sampling (for the slowest mixing model parameter).
> > > > >
> > > > > But anyway, give the slice samplers a try, and hopefully that will raise up the ESS values you're getting.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Jun 24, 2020 at 4:18 PM MIke Sparago <mikes...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > I have converted a GLM type model from JAGS to NIMBLE syntax. The model runs successfully with no errors, but the NIMBLE sample sizes are 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than JAGS.  I have tried block sampling on some of the obvious choices but not seeing any improvement.  I can see that JAGS is using slicer and conjugate normal samplers, so my next notion was to try and set the same samplers up in NIMBLE.  If there a more efficient way to at least get closer to the JAGS ESS?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > BTW - love the new NIMBLE cheat sheet!
> > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
I received the following warning message:

"Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 4.”

When running the following code below.  The program completes and the MCMC samples seem to be fine, so I’m wondering what is the cause of the warning?  Can I ignore the warning?

Thanks,
Brian

maskCode4_3 <- nimbleCode({
  ### Priors
  intercept~dnorm(0,sd=1000)
  maleEffect~dnorm(0,sd = 1000)
  ageEffect[1] <-0
  ageMaleI[1] <-0
  sigma_RE ~ dunif(0, 1000)

  for(i in 2:4) {
    # Priors for age effect and age:male interaction
    ageEffect[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
    ageMaleI[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
  }

  for(g in 1:8) {
    # Priors for business random effect
    b[g] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma_RE)
  }

  ### logit link and Bernoulli data probabilities
  for(i in 1:N) {

    logit(mask_prob[i]) <- intercept + maleEffect*male[i] +
      ageClassBase[i]*ageEffect[ageClass[i]] + male[i]*ageMaleI[ageClass[i]] +
      b[bGroup[i]]
    mask[i] ~ dbern(mask_prob[i])
  }

  ### Derived quantities
  # Odds ratios
  maleOdds<-exp(maleEffect)
  youngOdds<-exp(ageEffect[2])
  middleOdds<-exp(ageEffect[3])
  elderOdds<-exp(ageEffect[4])
  maleYoungOdds<-exp(ageMaleI[2])
  maleMiddleOdds<-exp(ageMaleI[3])
  maleElderOdds<-exp(ageMaleI[4])
})

mydataWOna<-mydata[!is.na <http://is.na>(mydata$gender_factor) & !is.na <http://is.na>(mydata$age_factor),]
maskConsts <- list(N = dim(mydataWOna)[1],
                   ageClassBase=ifelse(as.integer(mydataWOna$age_factor)>1,1,0),
                   ageClass=as.integer(mydataWOna$age_factor),
                   male=as.integer(mydataWOna$gender_factor)-1,
                   bGroup=as.integer(mydataWOna$business_factor)
)
maskData <- list(mask = mydataWOna$wearing_mask)

maskInits <- list(
  list(intercept = 0.5, maleEffect = 0.1,
       ageEffect=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3),
       ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)+10,
       b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4),
       sigma_RE=20 ),
  list(intercept = 1, maleEffect = 1,
       ageEffect=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)+0.1,
       ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)+0.1,
       b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4)-10,
       sigma_RE=10 ),
  list(intercept = 2, maleEffect = -1,
       ageEffect=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)-0.1,
       ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)-0.1,
       b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4)+10,
       sigma_RE=30 ),
  list(intercept = -1, maleEffect = -0.1,
       ageEffect=0.3,
       ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)-30,
       b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4)+0.3,
       sigma_RE=25+20 )
)

mcmc43.1.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = maskCode4_3, data = maskData, inits = maskInits,
                       monitors = c("intercept", "maleEffect","ageEffect",
                                    "ageMaleI","b","sigma_RE",
                                    "maleOdds","youngOdds","middleOdds",
                                    "elderOdds","maleYoungOdds","maleMiddleOdds",
                                    "maleElderOdds"),
                       thin = 100,
                       niter = 2000000, nburnin=10000,
                       nchains = 4, setSeed = FALSE,
                       constants = maskConsts,samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE)

Brian Beckage, Ph.D.
Professor
Department of Plant Biology
Department of Computer Science
Fellow, Gund Institute for Environment

messages.body_plain:
hi Brian,

You're initializing ageEffect with one value instead of four values in the fourth component of the inits list.

chris

On Mon, Jun 29, 2020 at 7:45 PM Brian Beckage <Brian....@uvm.edu> wrote:

> I received the following warning message:
>
> "Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 4.”
>
> When running the following code below.  The program completes and the MCMC samples seem to be fine, so I’m wondering what is the cause of the warning?  Can I ignore the warning?
>
> Thanks,
> Brian
>
>
> maskCode4_3 <- nimbleCode({
>   ### Priors
>   intercept~dnorm(0,sd=1000)
>   maleEffect~dnorm(0,sd = 1000)
>   ageEffect[1] <-0
>   ageMaleI[1] <-0
>   sigma_RE ~ dunif(0, 1000)
>
>   for(i in 2:4) {
>     # Priors for age effect and age:male interaction
>     ageEffect[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
>     ageMaleI[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
>   }
>
>   for(g in 1:8) {
>     # Priors for business random effect
>     b[g] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma_RE)
>   }
>
>   ### logit link and Bernoulli data probabilities
>   for(i in 1:N) {
>
>     logit(mask_prob[i]) <- intercept + maleEffect*male[i] +
>       ageClassBase[i]*ageEffect[ageClass[i]] + male[i]*ageMaleI[ageClass[i]] +
>       b[bGroup[i]]
>     mask[i] ~ dbern(mask_prob[i])
>   }
>
>   ### Derived quantities
>   # Odds ratios
>   maleOdds<-exp(maleEffect)
>   youngOdds<-exp(ageEffect[2])
>   middleOdds<-exp(ageEffect[3])
>   elderOdds<-exp(ageEffect[4])
>   maleYoungOdds<-exp(ageMaleI[2])
>   maleMiddleOdds<-exp(ageMaleI[3])
>   maleElderOdds<-exp(ageMaleI[4])
> })
>
>
> mydataWOna<-mydata[!is.na <http://is.na>(mydata$gender_factor) & !is.na <http://is.na>(mydata$age_factor),]
> maskConsts <- list(N = dim(mydataWOna)[1],
>                    ageClassBase=ifelse(as.integer(mydataWOna$age_factor)>1,1,0),
>                    ageClass=as.integer(mydataWOna$age_factor),
>                    male=as.integer(mydataWOna$gender_factor)-1,
>                    bGroup=as.integer(mydataWOna$business_factor)
> )
> maskData <- list(mask = mydataWOna$wearing_mask)
>
> maskInits <- list(
>   list(intercept = 0.5, maleEffect = 0.1,
>        ageEffect=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3),
>        ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)+10,
>        b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4),
>        sigma_RE=20 ),
>   list(intercept = 1, maleEffect = 1,
>        ageEffect=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)+0.1,
>        ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)+0.1,
>        b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4)-10,
>        sigma_RE=10 ),
>   list(intercept = 2, maleEffect = -1,
>        ageEffect=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)-0.1,
>        ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)-0.1,
>        b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4)+10,
>        sigma_RE=30 ),
>   list(intercept = -1, maleEffect = -0.1,
>        ageEffect=0.3,
>        ageMaleI=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3)-30,
>        b=c(0,0.1,0.2,0.3,-0.1,-0.5,-0.3,0.4)+0.3,
>        sigma_RE=25+20 )
> )
>
>
> mcmc43.1.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = maskCode4_3, data = maskData, inits = maskInits,
>                        monitors = c("intercept", "maleEffect","ageEffect",
>                                     "ageMaleI","b","sigma_RE",
>                                     "maleOdds","youngOdds","middleOdds",
>                                     "elderOdds","maleYoungOdds","maleMiddleOdds",
>                                     "maleElderOdds"),
>                        thin = 100,
>                        niter = 2000000, nburnin=10000,
>                        nchains = 4, setSeed = FALSE,
>                        constants = maskConsts,samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE)
>
>
>
>
>
> Brian Beckage, Ph.D.
> Professor
> Department of Plant Biology
> Department of Computer Science
> Fellow, Gund Institute for Environment
>
